meta.title: Crude unit pipe rupture and fire
meta.location: Chevron Richmond Refinery, #4 Crude Unit, California, USA (CSB public report)
meta.rules:
Look at the problem, not at blaming people.
One person talks at a time.
Every idea goes on the diagram first. We test ideas later.
Say how you know: facts beat opinions.
Off-topic points go to the parking lot.

problem.what: The 8-inch 4-sidecut line (light gas oil) ruptured; the release formed a vapour cloud that ignited
problem.where: #4 Crude Unit, 4-sidecut piping from the C-1100 atmospheric column, Chevron Richmond Refinery
problem.when: 6 August 2012, leak found about 15:50, ignition about 18:30
problem.extent: 19 employees engulfed in the vapour cloud, 6 minor injuries; about 15 000 people from the community sought medical treatment
problem.expected: The line stays intact until it is inspected or replaced; a leak is made safe without exposing people

facts.text: About 15:50 an outside operator found drips of diesel-like liquid from an insulated pipe about 4 m above ground: the 4-sidecut line. It could not be isolated from the process.
The leak was about 40 drips per minute. The supervisor and shift team leader judged it not significant enough to require a shutdown, but serious, and called the refinery fire department.
Firefighters arrived about 16:07, set up incident command and taped off a hot zone of about 6 m by 6 m around the leak.
About 40 people gathered at the leak over the next hours. A leak repair contractor was called to assess clamping the line.

Inspectors told the group the 4-sidecut walls were thinning from sulfidation corrosion, but data from two months before showed enough wall thickness to last to the 2016 turnaround. The group thought a local cause, such as wear at a pipe support, was likely.

The group decided to remove the insulation to find the leak ("daylighting"). A scaffold was built and two firefighters removed sheathing; soaked insulation caught fire and was put out. Hose streams then knocked off insulation and the leak worsened to a spray.
Some firefighters believed the line ran at about 54 °C. The actual temperature was close to 340 °C, near the autoignition temperature of the light gas oil.
Some people were uneasy and some suggested a shutdown, but left the decision to the managers present. No one used Stop Work Authority. Chevron had no leak response protocol.

Managers then decided to shut the unit down. A vapour cloud engulfed 19 people in the hot and cold zones; it ignited about two minutes later. 18 escaped just before ignition; a firefighter in the fire engine made his way out through the flames in full protective gear.
The ruptured part was a 1.3 m (52-inch) component of the 8-inch line, ASTM A53B carbon steel installed in 1976, original wall about 8.2 mm. Near the rupture it had lost on average 90 % of its wall.

The ruptured component contained 0.01 % silicon. Six of 12 samples from the line had less than 0.10 %. Low-silicon carbon steel can corrode up to 16 times faster by sulfidation. A53B has no minimum silicon content.
Thickness readings on the line were taken at monitoring points on higher-silicon fittings. In 2011, 12 points were added, but none on the component that failed.
In 2011 much of the 12-inch part of the same 4-sidecut line was replaced because it was too thin. The 8-inch part was judged fit to run.

A 2009 internal Chevron report recommended inspecting every component of high-temperature carbon steel piping like this line (100 % component inspection). It was not done on the 4-sidecut before 2012.
Requests to replace the 8-inch line in the 2007 and 2011 turnarounds were turned down under the turnaround scope criteria (the "Framing Document").
